More generally, if $\omega_{f,p}(t)$ has a known upper bound that tends to zero as $t\downarrow0$, we obtain a stopping rule for adaptive depth selection. We can stop at the first depth where the error bound meets the desired tolerance and later append layers to meet a tighter tolerance while keeping all earlier maps and readouts fixed.

papers.title: Exact SU(2) Yang-Mills Waves from a Simple Ansatz
papers.abstract: We use an ansatz based on rotations of the Pauli basis to construct exact propagating solutions of the sourceless SU(2) Yang--Mills equations in $(3+1)$ dimensions. By examining and extending this ansatz, we obtain two wave families with nontrivial transverse structures and a family of finite-amplitude waves on a self-similar non-Abelian background. These solutions can retain a genuinely non-Abelian structure while admitting arbitrary wave profiles propagating at the speed of light and carrying the corresponding longitudinal electric or magnetic fields. We also investigate the parameter conditions for their non-Abelian character and their energy transport. For the self-similar family, we study the structure of its singular plane and construct suitable sources to replace the singular region while preserving wave propagation in the remaining regions. This offers a possible interpretation of these solutions as propagating fields outside sources.

papers.title: Hugoniot Relation for Multi-Temperature Euler Equations of Compressible Plasma Flows
papers.abstract: Shock solutions for multi-temperature Euler equations are inherently ambiguous due to the loss of microscopic physical detail during model reduction and occurrence of non-conservative terms. This paper presents a detailed analytical study of shock structures in such models. We present two distinct Hugoniot relations, each corresponding to a physically admissible shock solution. Through classical analysis \`a la Courant--Friedrichs, we demonstrate that both satisfy admissibility conditions, revealing a fundamental non-uniqueness in shock structures. By relating these solutions to existing numerical schemes, the structure-preserving and vanishing viscosity approaches, we provide physically justified references for constructing and evaluating discontinuous numerical approximations. In particular, we emphasize that the Hugoniot relation is not uniquely determined by the macroscopic PDEs alone, but must be supplied from external sources such as experiments or first-principles simulations. This insight demonstrates the essential role of microscopic physics in resolving shock ambiguity and contributes to the theoretical foundation for modeling discontinuous plasma flows.

papers.title: A Spectral Framework for Closed-Form Relative Density Estimation
papers.abstract: We propose a closed-form spectral framework for relative log-density estimation in linearly parameterized probabilistic models, including unnormalized and conditional models. This is achieved by representing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence as an integral of weighted chi-squared divergences, converting KL estimation into a family of least-squares problems. We derive an explicit spectral formula based only on first- and second-order feature moments, yielding closed-form estimators of both divergences and log-density potentials for fixed features. The framework extends to a broad class of $f$-divergences and can be combined with kernelization or feature learning with neural networks (with then only a closed form for the last layer). We prove convergence guarantees for the resulting estimators and empirically compare them on synthetic data with optimization-based variational formulations, including logistic and softmax regression for normalized conditional models.

papers.title: Rare events of small-noise Doob conditioned processes
papers.abstract: Doob fixed-time conditioning enables the sampling of rare trajectories of Markov processes by modifying the drift so that reaching a prescribed target at a given time is guaranteed. We study the statistics of this conditioned path ensemble through the moment generating function in the weak-noise large deviation regime. Since the Doob drift is rarely available in closed form, we reinterpret the conditioned ensemble as the original process post-selected on the terminal constraint, thereby avoiding explicit construction of the Doob transform. This viewpoint then yields an optimal-control representation for the leading exponential contribution to the generating function, expressed as a variational principle with terminal boundary conditions set by the Doob end-point constraint. We illustrate the framework with two analytical examples and with an application to heat dissipation under Doob-controlled dynamics in a minimal model of biomolecular folding.

papers.title: Filtering out Erratic Observables: Wormholes from Gauging Nonlocal Symmetries
papers.abstract: The wormhole contribution to the gravitational path integral may be interpreted as smooth remnant of correlations among the erratic large-$N$ behaviors of dual CFTs. In this work, we investigate this idea in (2+1)-dimensional gravity. We show that one-sided boundary gravitons are intrinsically incomplete in the sense that the associated observable algebra has a nontrivial center regardless of choices of boundary conditions. Based on asymptotic symmetries, we bootstrap a general Poisson bracket to construct completions of the boundary gravitons. In the simplest completion, the commutant of the boundary graviton observable algebra is given by an observable algebra of monodromy data which we interpret as an effective description of one-sided black holes. We show that, to describe Lorentzian multi-boundary wormholes, only the monodromy data with a positivity restriction is needed. The positivity restriction results in emergent erratic large-$N$ behaviors for some observables. We filter out the erratic observables by restricting to a subspace on which they act trivially. The monodromy observables generate nonlocal symmetries lack of corresponding local currents. We show that gauging the nonlocal symmetries is equivalent to filtering out the erratic observables. For one CFT, gauging the nonlocal symmetries at the quantum level removes all black hole states. Filtering the partition function of CFTs leads to an apparent ensemble averaging. For two CFTs, a Hilbert subspace describing wormholes survives after gauging global part of the nonlocal symmetries. The filtered partition function of the two CFTs is an ensemble average over quantum gates entangling the monodromy degrees of freedom of the two CFTs. The correlation between the erratic observables of the two CFTs is preserved, which contributes to the filtered partition function as a wormhole term.

papers.title: Learning Transfers: Kan Extensions of Topological Invariants of Learned Representations
papers.abstract: When a learned representation is reused for a new task, which of its structure should survive? A task is a small category, a change of task is a functor $J$, and the invariants of a trained representation form a functor $F$. The left Kan extension $\operatorname{Lan}_JF$ is the invariant that the source and the change of task force on the target: by its universal property, every comparison of the source with an observed target invariant factors through it. The transfer discrepancy is the largest distance, over the target objects, between this extension and the observed invariant. For persistent homology the extension is a cokernel over comma categories, and a functorial version of the discrepancy, which also compares the maps between target objects, is $1$-Lipschitz under interleavings. On finite samples the discrepancy is a bottleneck distance, computed without approximation. For data glued from two pieces whose exclusive parts lie farther apart than the filtration scale, a Mayer-Vietoris sequence identifies what extending homology loses, while extending chains loses nothing. For a merge of labelled point clouds, the degree-zero discrepancy vanishes if and only if some $1$-Lipschitz classifier has a margin above the filtration scale at every sample point. In experiments on sampled manifolds, trained encoders and pretrained image models, every exact prediction holds on every sample. The discrepancy of truncated invariants recovers a hidden merge of separated parts far above chance and tells the intended target of a merge from a permuted control, but across pretrained models it does not track the accuracy of a linear probe.

papers.title: LEAF: A Learning-Enabled ADMM Framework for Accelerated Convex Optimization
papers.authors: Binh Nguyen, Trinh Tran, Truong X. Nghiem
papers.abstract: We propose LEAF, a learning-enabled ADMM framework for accelerated convex optimization. The key idea is to approximate the Moreau envelope of the objective function using an Input Convex Neural Network (ICNN), resulting in a learned model that preserves convexity and smoothness. This leads to the proposed Moreau Envelope Learning ADMM (MEL-ADMM) and its splitting variant sMEL-ADMM. Unlike existing approaches that learn high-dimensional operators directly, LEAF learns a scalar-valued Moreau envelope, significantly reducing model complexity and improving data efficiency. The framework accommodates a broad class of convex problems with smooth and non-smooth objectives. By embedding convexity explicitly through the ICNN architecture, the proposed approach maintains high approximation accuracy while preserving key structural properties of the optimization problem. Both MEL-ADMM and sMEL-ADMM are developed with theoretical guarantees of convergence and feasibility under the learned model. Rigorous analysis shows that the proposed methods achieve convergence rates comparable to classical ADMM while reducing per-iteration computational cost. Numerical experiments demonstrate up to an order-of-magnitude speedup over state-of-the-art solvers while maintaining low optimality gaps

papers.title: Constraints on regular black holes with nonminimally coupled electromagnetic fields
papers.authors: Ana Bokuli\'c, Tajron Juri\'c, Luka Kanai Peji\'c, Filip Po\v{z}ar, Ivica Smoli\'c
papers.abstract: Construction of physically realistic theories admitting regular black hole solutions remains an important open problem in gravitational physics. While theories with electromagnetic fields minimally coupled to gravity have been extensively studied over the past two decades, theories with nonminimal couplings remain comparatively unexplored. We investigate theories containing the interaction terms $R F_{ab}F^{ab}$, $R_{ab} F^a_{\ \, c} \, F^{bc}$ and $R_{abcd} F^{ab} F^{cd}$, which generically arise in low-energy effective Lagrangians. We prove that magnetically charged regular black holes are excluded, except possibly for a special choice of coupling constants, and argue that a similar conclusion applies to electrically charged regular black holes. We further show that similar conclusions hold for Lagrangian terms of the form $f(R,F_{ab}{\star F}^{ab})$.

papers.title: Focused median bias reduction
papers.authors: Davide Benussi, Ioannis Kosmidis, Alessandra Salvan, Nicola Sartori
papers.abstract: Median bias reduction of maximum likelihood estimators can substantially improve estimation and inference. Existing generally applicable methods are, however, implicit, requiring the solution of nonlinear systems of estimating equations for a specified parameterization. Their application to parameter transformations often involves tedious algebra and bespoke implementations. We develop an explicit median bias-corrected estimator for focus parameters defined as smooth scalar transformations of the parameter. The estimator results from solving an equation derived from the Cornish-Fisher expansion of the centred and scaled maximum likelihood estimator of the focus parameter, and requires only the maximum likelihood or an asymptotically equivalent estimator of the model parameter, the gradient and Hessian of the transformation, and expectations of products of log-likelihood derivatives. These expectations are available for many models in the bias reduction literature and can also be estimated by Monte Carlo simulation. The resulting estimators are third-order median unbiased and provide one-step approximations to estimators from implicit median bias reduction when the focus is a component of the parameter. The method can improve standard asymptotic inference and enables hull-based confidence procedures to produce intervals with near nominal finite-sample coverage. We illustrate the framework with examples involving Mahalanobis distances, quantiles, focus parameters in regression, stratified, circular, and multiple-mediator models, and model selection settings using the Focused Information Criterion.

papers.title: Financial Resilience Evaluation: From Conditional Expectations to Dynamic Convex Risk Measures
papers.authors: Matteo Ferrari, Roger J. A. Laeven, Emanuela Rosazza Gianin, Marco Zullino
papers.abstract: Financial resilience concerns whether, and how rapidly, a risky position recovers or deteriorates at a future time $t$, given the information available at time $s\leq t$. As a first step, the resilience rate was introduced as the expected instantaneous rate of change of a price or risk-assessment process. Because this quantity captures only the conditional mean of future increments, it cannot distinguish between positions with the same expected recovery but different conditional risk profiles. We obtain a richer characterization by evaluating such increments through a possibly nonlinear dynamic risk measure $\rho$. For an It\^o process $\pi$ and a normalized, cash-additive $\rho$, we define the resilience evaluation as the $L^1$-limit of $\varepsilon^{-1}\rho_s(\pi_{t+\varepsilon}-\pi_t)$, as $\varepsilon\to 0^+$, whenever it exists. For a convex $\rho$ induced by BSDEs with Lipschitz or quadratic drivers, we prove existence and a dual representation: it is the worst-case conditional expectation, over zero-penalty measure changes, of an effective drift that combines the physical drift of $\pi$ with the risk adjustment assigned by $\rho$ to the volatility of $\pi$. We establish attainment of the optimal scenario and illustrate the scope of the construction and the role of the required assumptions through examples and counterexamples.

papers.title: Adaptive Reparametrized Time for Score-Based Diffusion Sampling
papers.authors: Yilie Huang, Wenpin Tang, Xun Yu Zhou
papers.abstract: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where the learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard, but their fixed, ad hoc prescriptions can be suboptimal. We propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating sampling-clock speed as the control, so a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in diffusion time and a leading-order Euler error surrogate defines the allocation objective. To solve the resulting high-dimensional deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized Gaussian-policy formulation that turns schedule learning into continuous-time reinforcement learning. We prove ART-RL is equivalent to ART at optimality: the mean of the optimal Gaussian policy solves ART. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor-critic updates. Experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation show that ART-learned schedules, when plugged into existing samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improve sample quality over strong baselines at matched budgets. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalizability, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, data sets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

papers.title: Bichromatic Geometric Spanners
papers.abstract:
For an edge-weighted graph $G=(V,E)$ and a stretch parameter $t\geq 1$, a $t$-spanner is a subgraph $H\subseteq G$ such that the shortest path distances in $G$ and $H$ satisfy $\delta_H(u,v)\leq t\, \delta_G(u,v)$ for all $u,v\in V$. In metric spanners, $V$ is a finite metric space, and $G$ is the complete graph with edge weights corresponding to the distances between the endpoints. When $G$ is the complete graph on $n$ points in the plane, $O(n)$-size $t$-spanners are possible for any $t>1$: For every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a $(1+\varepsilon)$-spanner with $O(n/\varepsilon)$ edges (i.e., the stretch can be arbitrarily close to 1).
  When $G=K(R,B)$ is the complete bipartite graph on $n$ bichromatic points in the plane, in general, no spanner construction can guarantee stretch $t<3$ with $o(n^2)$ edges. Bose et al.~(SICOMP 2009) constructed a $(3+\varepsilon)$-spanner with $O(n\log n)$ edges for any constant $\varepsilon>0$. Our main result is a new construction for a $(3+\varepsilon)$-spanner with $O(\sqrt{1/\varepsilon}\cdot n)$ edges. Eliminating the $O(\log n)$ factor resolves a problem left open for more than 17 years, and raises a new research problem about optimizing the dependence on $\varepsilon$. When off-metric Steiner points are allowed, no Steiner spanner construction can guarantee stretch $t<2$ with $o(n^2)$ edges, and we construct a bipartite Steiner $(2+\varepsilon)$-spanner for $K(R,B)$ with $O(\sqrt{1/\varepsilon}\cdot n)$ edges.
  We also study (non-Steiner) spanners for $G=K(R,B)$ on $n$ bichromatic points on the real line: In this case, we show that the MST of $K(R,B)$ is a 7-spanner, and we construct a 3-spanner with at most $2n-3$ edges.

papers.title: WarpMPC: Large-Batch MPC on GPU via ADMM with Unrolled $LDL^\top$ Factorization
papers.authors: Henrik Hose, Se Hwan Jeon, Charles Khazoom, Sangbae Kim, Sebastian Trimpe
papers.abstract: This paper introduces numerical optimizations for maximizing throughput on GPU when solving large batches (10,000 to over 100,000) of sequential quadratic programming (SQP) iterations, where all problems have the same structure. The optimizations are implemented in a toolbox WarpMPC for model-predictive control (MPC) in JAX and Warp. Based on the insight that all MPC problem instances in a batch share the same sparsity in time, cost, and constraints, we propose unrolling sparse linear factorizations and solves, which dominate alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) solver runtime. We avoid memory access bottlenecks and wasting computations via optimized memory layout, padding-reducing segmentation of the unrolled factorization, and dependency level scheduled backsolves, additionally accelerating sensitivity computation. We achieve throughputs of 8,000 to 250,000 SQP iterations per second on nonlinear cartpole, quadrotor, and humanoid robot benchmarks, outperforming baselines by 3$\times$ to 25$\times$. We illustrate practical usefulness by synthesizing a dataset and training a neural network approximation of an MPC in under 5 minutes that stabilizes a nano quadrotor in hardware experiments.

papers.title: One Shot, Twenty-One Balls: A Computer-Assisted Proof of a Single-Stroke Total Clearance in an Idealized Model of Snooker
papers.abstract: Snooker folklore holds that no single stroke can pocket all twenty-one object balls. We examine the claim in an explicit model: twenty-two equal disks on a rectangle with six pocket points, under constant rolling deceleration, frictionless collisions with normal restitution, and lossy specular cushions. We exhibit a configuration and a stroke, and prove in interval arithmetic that every stroke in an explicit box around it pockets all twenty-one object balls, so the set of successful strokes has positive measure. That set is a ribbon: every speed from 9.3214 to 12 m/s works, while the certified window of directions is 9.481e-43 radians wide, a number explained by a first-order analysis of twenty near-grazing collisions. A second configuration, a near-frozen cluster, has a certified window 9.4e-4 radians wide, thirty-nine orders of magnitude wider; its certificate uses Taylor models of degree six. The strokes with a given list of events form a semialgebraic set, and the endpoints of the windows are algebraic points of the circle. For the regulation opening position we state the corresponding conjecture, and show that if it holds with a regular witness then a finite certified search establishes it.

papers.title: Load-induced Taylor-Aris dispersion in compliant electroosmotic pumps with viscoelastic electrolytes
papers.authors: Subhajyoti Sahoo, Ameeya Kumar Nayak, Kirti Chandra Sahu
papers.abstract: We investigate the dispersion of a passive, neutral solute in a compliant slit, in which electroosmotic flow drives a viscoelastic electrolyte against an outlet pressure load. The electrolyte is modelled using the simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner model with an inviscid Newtonian solvent. Combining lubrication theory, Debye Huckel linearisation and a local elastic-foundation model, we determine the loaded flow and quantify solute dispersion. A central finding is that hydraulic loading fundamentally alters the thin-electric-double-layer limit of shear dispersion. It was observed that shear dispersion vanishes under free-flow conditions, but an adverse pressure gradient continues to support core shear under load, resulting in a finite dispersion plateau even without flow reversal. This plateau increases with hydraulic loading and is further enhanced by viscoelasticity at a fixed throughput fraction. For Newtonian flow, wall expansion leaves the plateau unchanged under constant-current conditions but increases it under constant-voltage conditions. At finite EDL thicknesses, opposing electroosmotic and pressure-driven shear can partially cancel, improving the plate number despite reduced throughput. The combined effects of shear dispersion, molecular diffusion and transit time produce an optimal EDL thickness at prescribed throughput. Joint optimisation shifts the optimum towards free-flow conditions and thinner EDLs for the range of parameters considered. The predicted plate numbers agree closely with Brownian-dynamics simulations for six benchmark cases. These results establish the role of hydraulic loading and wall compliance in controlling the trade-off between pressure delivery and band broadening in compliant electroosmotic pumps.

papers.title: Quasi-SVD: Learning a Lie-constrained matrix factorisation for real-time imaging
papers.abstract: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) underlies matrix factorisation tasks across many fields, with imaging applications demanding cost-efficient processing. Yet SVD algorithms are inherently sequential, constraining GPU throughput and limiting online deployment in imaging pipelines. This study introduces a fully parallelized matrix factorization framework for GPUs by enforcing matrix orthogonality on left singular vectors via Lie-parametrised algebra and recovering the remaining components through soft constraints. This asymmetric constraint design enables an efficient parallel decomposition with an orthogonal left factor, achieves high reconstruction fidelity and substantially accelerates computation relative to the exact SVD, with high throughput exceeding standard video frame rates. Performance is evaluated on multiple imaging tasks spanning complementary computational regimes: (1) an MNIST denoising benchmark at an intermediate scale with known ground truth, (2) Mueller matrix polarimetry for neurosurgical tissue characterisation, requiring massive batch processing of small matrices, and (3) spatio-temporal background subtraction for ultrasound localisation microscopy, requiring high-dimensional matrix separation. Across regimes and instruments, the proposed framework demonstrates robust domain transfer at various matrix scales and 2.6--67$\times$ speed-ups over the exact GPU SVD, and, unlike randomised SVD, accelerates large batches of small full-rank matrices. By prioritising downstream reconstruction fidelity over exact spectral recovery, the proposed SVD framework enables GPU-friendly matrix factorisation.

papers.title: Stochastic partial differential equation model for environmental DNA dynamics in river environments
papers.abstract: Environmental DNA (eDNA) has emerged as a novel tool for quantifying the seasonal abundance of aquatic species in water bodies; however, its mathematical modeling is still at a germinating stage because of its mechanistic uncertainties. We propose a first-step mathematical and computational framework for the eDNA dynamics of migratory fish based on a novel stochastic partial differential equation model with a delayed source input. The model governs spatiotemporal eDNA concentration in rivers where the source comes from a stochastic differential equation for the migration dynamics of the fish. The affine nature of the model facilitates its theoretical analysis, including the guarantee of well-posedness and the closed-form derivation of the Laplace functional despite the proportionality coefficient of the multiplicative noise term being non-Lipschitz. We also propose a discretization scheme for the model that theoretically generates nonnegative numerical solutions. We finally apply the proposed model to eDNA concentration data sampled from midstream reaches of a river system and perform sensitivity analysis.

papers.title: The M/PH_2/1 Queue: Explicit Distributions, Sojourn Times and Numerical Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Two-phase phase-type ($PH_2$) distributions are among the service-time models used most often in applied queueing, because they capture coefficients of variation above and below one with few parameters. This note collects, in one place and in ready-to-use form, the stationary queue-length distribution $p_n = A_1 r_1^n + A_2 r_2^n$ and the sojourn-time density $f_{W_s}(t) = c_1 e^{\alpha_1 t} + c_2 e^{\alpha_2 t}$ for the $M/E_2/1$, $M/Hypo_2/1$, $M/Hyper_2/1$ and $M/Coxian_2/1$ queues, with every coefficient written in the parameters that a fitting procedure returns. None of these results is new in substance; however, obtaining them from the general theory takes work that each user would otherwise have to repeat. The formulas are obtained from the Pollaczek-Khinchine transforms, related to the matrix-geometric and phase-type representations of the same queues, and verified numerically in 40-digit arithmetic. The note also gives the matrices needed to reproduce the results in standard software, a comparison with the matrix-analytic library BuTools, formulas for tail and threshold quantities and their derivatives, and a worked example calibrated to published surgical-time data.

papers.title: K\"ahler landscapes for complex neural network descents and guarantees including a search and destroy of the Calabi-Yau manifold
papers.abstract: We study landscapes for complex-parameterized networks. Our approach is motivated with an information-theoretic manifold perspective of the parameter and via classical optimization guarantees although of complex geometric variety such as through Dolbeault asymptotics. The descent path admits a K\"ahler information metric under a cross-entropy via the Wirtinger Hessian on the log-likelihood potential. We descend according to a differentiated loss scaled by the inverse metric, so the descent path remains in the holomorphic tangent bundle. We emphasize information manifolds which profane theoretical guarantees via ill-curvature-conditioned, or lack thereof, landscapes. We focus on Calabi-Yau metrics specifically in a non-compact setting with a global potential, so defined geometrically rather than invoking the topological requirements of the Calabi conjecture. In non-compact settings, we can write the metric determinant with respect to a background in terms of a function, pluriharmonic or real. Using Yau's Liouville theorem, we get a small eigenvalue blow-up effect under nontrivial background interaction, geometric invariance of the endomorphism constant, and almost low rank assumptions. In an empirical setting, a Ricci-flat metric will not form, but large eigenvalues can be a local condition and hold empirically on open sets even in generalized K\"ahler cases due to lower bounds on the Ricci potential. Moreover, it has been discovered that negative curvature subverts the loss landscape, specifically sectional curvature, so we expand on this and draw interconnections to negative-definite Ricci curvature. Our arguments primarily exist via geometric modality, although we establish roots in deep learning theory such as through asymptotics at initialization and connections through failure modes of neural network guarantees under vanishing and negative Ricci curvature.

papers.title: Nucleation and propagation of brittle fracture as a constrained energy minimization problem
papers.authors: Oscar Lopez-Pamies, Farhad Kamarei, Gilles A. Francfort, Alessandro Giacomini
papers.abstract: This paper presents a macroscopic, or continuum, theory aimed at describing when, where, and why cracks nucleate and propagate in nominally elastic brittle materials under monotonic, quasi-static, but otherwise arbitrary mechanical loads. Motivated by recent insights, the proposed sharp theory posits that: \emph{cracks nucleate and propagate exclusively in regions where the strength surface of the material is exceeded, with their evolution dictated by the minimization of the sum of the potential --- the elastic energy minus the work done by the externally applied forces --- and surface energies.} While the theory applies to materials with any elasticity (linear or nonlinear) and any material symmetry (isotropic or anisotropic), attention is restricted here to the most basic case of isotropic elastic brittle materials. For demonstration purposes, the theory is confronted with a set of nine tests that span the entire range of well-settled experimental knowledge on fracture nucleation and propagation --- the so-called ``Nine Circles of Elastic Brittle Fracture'' --- on both a hard material (a silicate glass) and a soft material (a synthetic rubber).

papers.title: Comparison of Algebraic Block Multi-Coloring and Leiden Methods for Parallel Preconditioning in the ICCG Method
papers.abstract: In the application of incomplete Cholesky preconditioning to the incomplete Cholesky-conjugate gradient (ICCG) method, forward and backward substitutions exhibit sequential dependencies that constitute a major bottleneck for parallelization in multicore environments. To alleviate this bottleneck, the algebraic block multi-coloring (ABMC) method achieves both parallelism and data locality through block-wise coloring. However, ABMC requires the number of blocks to be specified as an input parameter in advance. This study evaluates the Leiden method as an alternative blocking approach for parallel preconditioning in the ICCG method. As a community detection technique that maximizes a quality function for graph partitioning, the Leiden method automatically generates blocks that reflect the matrix structure without requiring the number of blocks a priori. We partition the adjacency graphs of sparse matrices using the Leiden method and utilize the resulting blocks for parallel preconditioning. We implement the Leiden method using modularity and the constant Potts model as quality functions and compare its performance with that of the ABMC method in terms of the number of iterations, execution time, and L2 cache efficiency across eight symmetric positive definite matrices. The experimental results demonstrate that the Leiden method with the constant Potts model achieves performance comparable to that of the ABMC method configured with an optimized number of blocks.

papers.title: Differential equations for Dotsenko--Fateev integrals: the case of degenerate fields $\Phi_{n,1}$
papers.abstract: We study higher-order differential equations corresponding to integrals of the Dotsenko--Fateev type and associated with four-point correlation functions with degenerate fields $\Phi_{n,1}$. We determine the general structure and coefficients of the equations in terms of the integral parameters $ \{ A,B,C,g \} $. In particular, special cases of these equations in CFT are used for verification. In addition, the relationship between higher-order differential equations and hypergeometric operators is established.

papers.title: A high-order ghost-point immersed boundary method with auxiliary differential equations for time-domain impedance walls
papers.authors: Abdoulaye Ouattara, David Marx, Christian Prax
papers.abstract: This paper presents a method for performing time-domain simulations of a sound field interacting with a wall having a locally-reacting impedance. The linearized Euler equations are solved using a high-order finite difference method. To impose the impedance condition on a wall that is not aligned with the Cartesian grid, an immersed boundary method (IBM) is employed. It relies on a ghost-point approach with a normal-stencil-based reconstruction, where the impedance is accounted for via auxiliary differential equations (ADEs), which are integrated using the same Runge-Kutta scheme as the governing equations. The method is validated against semi-analytical solutions for a pressure pulse reflecting off a flat or cylindrical wall with an impedance corresponding to a mass-spring-damper system. The cylindrical case solution is derived in the appendix. The measured convergence order is approximately 4 for a flat wall and just slighlty smaller for a curved wall. Long-term stability is verified by the diffraction of a monopole by a cylinder.

papers.title: When Should a Human Take Back Control? Optimal Delegation under Turbulent AI Risk
papers.authors: Haoze Yan, Julien Roze, Ved Upadhyay, Unal Tatar, Thibaut Mastrolia
papers.abstract: When should a human take control from an autonomous AI agent, how much checking is worthwhile, and when should autonomy resume? These decisions become harder when incidents cluster and recent errors signal elevated risk. Exploratory analyses of AgentLogs coding-agent traces and ODCV-Bench task runs show higher held-out log likelihood for Hawkes incident-history models than matched no-history baselines, with positive gains whose conditional $90\%$ intervals exclude zero. AgentLogs evaluates continuous-time incident timing and type; ODCV evaluates failure occurrence at discrete decisions. Motivated by this predictive evidence, we formulate a continuous-time delegation problem that jointly chooses productive action, verification effort, and switching rates between human-directed, AI-assisted operation and autonomous AI operation. The model assumes that verification weakens incident propagation and balances project benefits against operating, supervision, risk, and handoff costs. Our Hawkes-PPO method summarizes observed incidents with exponential memory filters and learns these decisions from rewards. In synthetic experiments, it achieves a higher evaluated objective than either fixed regime and PPO without history filters, and approaches an approximate full-information benchmark. Further experiments show how incident excitation and supervision costs shape delegation.

papers.title: ProofLoom: Proof-Obligation-Driven Theory Construction for Autoformalizing Research-Level Stochastic Optimization
papers.authors: Feiming Wang, Daibo Li, Kun Yuan
papers.abstract: Formalizing research-level stochastic optimization in Lean requires both an algorithm model and domain theory connecting foundational libraries to convergence proofs. Revising a model to restore provability can change the mathematical claim. We introduce ProofLoom, a fully automated LLM-agent system for Proof-Obligation-Driven Theory Construction. Given a published algorithm, target theorem, and source proof, ProofLoom autonomously constructs the Lean model and supporting theory. Open proof obligations drive the development of definitions, interfaces, lemmas, and proof plans. Signature contracts record evidence and obligations for model revisions; an independent Judge rejects unsupported assumptions and weakened conclusions. Planner expands the published argument into intermediate claims, and Audit checks whether the Lean proof follows it. Across tasks, SOptLib accumulates verified mathematics and construction experience: reusable results are extracted, generalized, and verified, while modeling decisions and failed proof routes are recorded. Later tasks retrieve these results and records and contribute new developments, forming a cycle of construction, accumulation, and reuse. On fifteen textbook and research-paper tasks, ProofLoom obtains mean human ratings of 6.3/7 and 6.4/7, compared with 4.9/7 and 5.0/7 for the strongest of six baselines. Across 33 developments, it produces 490,693 lines of algorithm-local Lean code with no sorry. The formalizations also expose 28 incorrect formulas, proof gaps, and algorithm-analysis mismatches in published sources across 22 developments, each with checked evidence.

papers.title: Rounded Clocks and Finite Precision: A Transfer Principle Between Continuous and Discrete Quantum Dynamics
papers.abstract: I present a short approach to discretizing continuous unitary evolution in finite dimensions. For a time-dependent Hamiltonian $H(s)$ with $s\in[0,1]$ and an integer $T\ge1$, let $U(T)$ be the evolution of $H(t/T)$ over time $T$, and let $W_T=e^{-iH((T-1)/T)}\cdots e^{-iH(0)}$ be the product of the unitaries generated by its samples. With a half-step phase at each end, $V(T)=e^{-iH(1)/2}W_Te^{iH(0)/2}$ is the evolution generated by $H(\lfloor t+1/2\rfloor/T)$, where $\lfloor t+1/2\rfloor$ is a rounded clock, time at finite precision. Whereas Duhamel's formula only bounds $\|V(T)-U(T)\|$ by a constant, I show that $\|V(T)-U(T)\|=O(1/T)$ in operator norm, with explicit constants, whenever $H'$ is Lipschitz and every sample has eigenvalue differences at most a fixed width below $2\pi$. The gain comes from cancellation within and between time steps. This general transfer theorem assumes neither adiabaticity nor a spectral gap, and any operator-norm bound for $U(T)$ transfers to $V(T)$ with an added $O(1/T)$. Nonetheless, discrete adiabatic theorems for $W_T$ follow from continuous ones, because the end phases commute with the spectral projectors of $H(0)$ and $H(1)$. For a product of samples of a $C^2$ unitary family, a continuously moving arc of fixed length $\vartheta$ that avoids the spectrum determines a Hermitian logarithm meeting the width condition, and the $O(1/T)$ bound has coefficients $O(\vartheta^{-3})$. In the easier direction, Duhamel's formula shows that rounding the clock to midpoints and truncating the entries of a regulated time-dependent Hamiltonian at a fixed binary place gives a product within $T$ times the error of the rounded, truncated Hamiltonian.

papers.title: Primal/Dual Method for the Grothendieck Constant
papers.authors: Steven Heilman, Chris Jones, Giulio Malavolta
papers.abstract: We determine the hundredths digit of the real Grothendieck constant by proving $1.773 \leq K_G \leq 1.7799$. Furthermore, numerical heuristics suggest the estimate $K_G \approx 1.779$. We start by simplifying the Gaussian duality theory of $K_G$, based on Hermite projection games and Krivine rounding schemes. The bounds are obtained by a heuristic primal/dual search for these objects, followed by rigorous {\em certification} of their values. The search and certification are performed using AI tools, and in particular the rigorous certificates are very large (analytical reductions to thousands of numerical inequalities).

papers.title: Explaining the Saliency Map Sparsity of Adversarially-Trained Neural Networks
papers.authors: Yannick Lunk, Atell Yehor Krasnopolsky, Damien Garreau, Leon Bungert
papers.abstract: Understanding why deep neural networks make a given prediction is of great importance for their safe deployment. In computer vision, saliency maps, which highlight the image region most influential for a prediction, remain a widely-used form of explanation. An empirical observation is the apparent sparsity of gradient saliency maps of adversarially-trained neural networks. In this paper, we propose a theoretical explanation of this phenomenon for two-layer ReLU networks. We build on the established equivalence of adversarial training to the minimization of the empirical risk with weight-decay penalization and an added adversarial total variation term -- valid for certain loss functions. As the number of data points and neurons grows and the regularization parameters are sent to zero at appropriate rates, we prove that minimizers converge to a Bayes classifier with minimal gradient and Barron norm. Sparsity appears since for adversarial training with $\ell_\infty$-attacks the gradient norm is anisotropic and favors axis-aligned / sparse gradients. We illustrate our theoretical findings experimentally by evaluating the gradient $\ell_1$-norm and thresholded sparsity of naturally versus adversarially trained models.

papers.title: Finite-time quantum equilibration from local correlations
papers.abstract: We study equilibration of a fixed subsystem coupled to an initially maximally mixed bath. We show that the worst-input mean-square error, maximised over observation windows of length $T$, is bounded from above and below by the mean square of a complete local autocorrelation on $[0,T]$. The constants depend only on the subsystem dimension, and no assumption on degeneracies of energies or energy gaps is required. Subtracting the stationary part of the correlation gives equilibration to the temporal state; retaining it gives thermalisation to the maximally mixed state. We then obtain explicit bounds for two static Hamiltonian families. A periodic spin-clock model thermalises on $O(n\log n)$ windows at fixed accuracy despite an exponentially small positive energy. A randomly dressed commuting model, with interaction range $O(\log N)$, has expected error $O(N^{-b}+T^{-1})$ while retaining an extensive family of conserved observables. We explain how the locally weighted spectrum determines these bounds.

papers.title: Self-organizing recruitment cascades couple Levy search to a clustered maximum-entropy resource field
papers.abstract: Foraging recruitment is modeled as a contagion: an agent finding a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade on the group's communication network. Because activation is degree-normalized, crowding shuts the cascade off, causing the swarm to aggregate on a resource and then disperse to explore again. Acting on the cascade moves agents in space, rewiring the network; recruitment and exploration are thus one coupled process, and removing this coupling alone abolishes self-limitation. Recruitment spreads only within a connectivity window bounded below by percolation onset and above by degree-blocking. The swarm self-organizes to the near-critical edge of this window--self-organized quasi-criticality--hovering near but below the critical point without settling onto a size-invariant critical state, with a finite-correlation-time activity spectrum (Lorentzian-like, not 1/f) consistent with local criticality. Recruitment raises harvest up to 2.7x over solitary search on sparse, clustered fields and loses (down to 0.37x) on abundant or uniform ones; because resources generically aggregate, the favourable regime is the common one. The Levy search and resource field are both least-committal: a maximum-caliber walk coupled to a maximum-entropy point process whose generic sign is clustered, with the optimal search exponent tracking the field's fractal dimension. Heavy-tailed Levy exploration crosses sparse voids while recruitment cascades exploit clusters by switching agents to short local steps, binding exploration and recruitment into a single self-organizing cycle.

papers.title: Avoid-or-Compress Words for Reachable Images Missing Four or Five States
papers.abstract: Given a set of states $S$ and a nonempty proper subset $A\subset S$, an avoid-or-compress word either omits a state of $A$ from the image of $S$ or reduces the size of that image. We determine the largest possible length of a shortest such word when $S$ is a reachable image missing four or five states. For strongly connected synchronizing automata, the answers are $\min(n-|A|,11)$ and $\min(n-|A|,14)$, respectively, and both are attained over a binary alphabet. The lower bounds follow from uniform constructions. For the upper bounds, short-pair graphs and the linear span of short images reduce the problem to finitely many configurations. A computer-assisted classification eliminates these configurations except for one complete bipartite graph, which is excluded by a combinatorial argument.

papers.title: Transport in spinful non-Hermitian gauge lattices
papers.authors: Hamed Ghaemi-Dizicheh, Shahram Dehdashti, Janis N\"otzel
papers.abstract: We extend the generalized transfer-matrix method introduced in [H. Ghaemi-Dizicheh, Phys.\ Rev.\ B \textbf{107}, 125155 (2023)] to one-dimensional spinful non-Hermitian tight-binding lattices with matrix-valued Abelian and non-Abelian gauge couplings. We derive a minimal channel-resolved transfer matrix and identify its eigenvalues with the generalized Bloch factors. The same transfer matrix determines the periodic- and open-boundary spectra, generalized Brillouin zone, skin localization, and finite-sample scattering conditions. In the Abelian limit, the model separates into fixed spin sectors, yielding exact spectral results and closed finite-length transport expressions in terms of Chebyshev polynomials. These results reveal bipolar spin-dependent skin localization and distinguish the reciprocal hopping scale, which governs poles, zeros, and reflectionlessness, from the directed-amplification factor controlling transmission asymmetry, transparency, and invisibility. For non-Abelian gauge fields, noncommuting link matrices coherently mix the spin sectors, such that four transfer eigenmodes jointly determine the non-Bloch spectrum and transport eigenchannels. We show that this mixing produces spin-hybridized lasing and coherent-perfect-absorption channels, Zeeman-tunable lasing thresholds, and direction-dependent reflectionless transport accompanied by pronounced spin conversion. The resulting boundary-condition criteria describe lasing, coherent perfect absorption, reflectionlessness, transparency, and invisibility, while identifying spin polarization and conversion as experimentally accessible signatures that distinguish Abelian from non-Abelian non-Hermitian transport.

papers.title: Ensembles of Random Partition-Based Models under Covariate Shift
papers.abstract: Distribution shifts, including covariate shifts, are ubiquitous in real-world applications of machine learning. Empirical evidence suggests that, across a variety of models with and without downstream adaptation, ensembles tend to be more robust to covariate shift than single models. We extend the theory of covariate shift severity from single models to ensembles, providing theoretical justification for the empirical trends. We introduce new discrepancy measures of covariate shift severity to control the risk of partition-based kernel estimators. We then show that with sufficient ensemble size, these models can achieve minimax-optimal risk convergence rates under covariate shift. Our results suggest that modelers can expect to need larger ensemble sizes for more severe covariate shifts.

papers.title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
papers.authors: Junbo Jacob Lian, Kaixuan Chen, Hanzhang Qin, Huiling Chen, Chaoyu Zhang, Chung-Piaw Teo
papers.abstract: Dantzig--Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying constraint families, and each candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, as in classical lot-sizing, network-design, and facility-location formulations. We prove that when an evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, methods that observe only bounds need of order $k^w$ evaluations to find a hidden group of $w$ families in the worst case. A prediction missing $e$ members reduces this to $\Theta(k^e)$ through a staged search that need not know $e$. The orders extend to several groups, prices, and growing evaluation costs. We study two predictors: a lookahead at an optimal LP dual, which vanishes on groups whose families share no variable, and language models reading the model, verified by the staged search in JointDW. Such groups appear in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved and in all 59 benchmark instances. Given the coefficients of constructed models with up to 16 families, one language model names a true group first in 249 of 252 answers. On the benchmark instances, decompositions chosen by language models from the text solve faster than those of GCG's detector.

papers.title: Thermochemical Rossby waves in rapid rotation: from swallowtail geometry to nonlinear selection
papers.abstract: When heat and solute both destabilise a rapidly rotating fluid, do their buoyancies add? Codensity models assume so, giving a straight onset diagonal; spherical shells show curved and kinked thresholds. We study the Busse-Simitev rotating annulus, whose normal modes obey an exact complex cubic dispersion relation. Combining the Bilharz criterion with the neutral-curve envelope yields, in the rapid-rotation limit, an explicit swallowtail wave front, in Arnold's sense, that bends the codensity diagonal into smooth and then kinked thresholds as the diffusivity ratio decreases. Its cusp edges lie inside the unstable domain and its exposed kink ends at the swallowtail singularity; these are singularities of wave-number selection, without coalescence of temporal eigenvalues, and the swallowtail diffusivity ratio has analytical small- and large-Prandtl-number limits. At a kink, broad, fast thermal and narrow, slow compositional Rossby waves become neutral together; hidden arcs mark the birth and merger of unstable wave-number bands. The same geometry enters nonlinear selection: mean-scalar feedback factors through neutral-arc normals and scalar responses, so the mean-profile coexistence margin is positive at every corner of the leading front and vanishes quadratically with the kink angle as the waves merge. Complete cubic coefficients predict robust coexistence at a reference corner and a narrow bistable interval near merger. Periodic-cell simulations away from merger confirm the coexisting waves and their invasion thresholds.

papers.title: Direct product geometries in $n$-dimensional linear and quadratic gravity
papers.abstract: Direct-product spacetimes offer a tractable route to exact solutions in gravity theories beyond general relativity. We study $n$-dimensional direct-product spacetimes of $(m_1+m_2)$, $(2+m)$, and $(2+\ldots+2)$ type in linear gravity and general pure quadratic-curvature gravity, allowing the two-dimensional subspaces to have nonconstant curvature. We classify the resulting solution spaces and determine how the allowed geometries depend on the gravitational theory, the dimension, and the curvature couplings. Metrics containing two-dimensional part(s) of nonconstant curvature are governed either by algebraic conditions on a curvature profile, or, in one special class of quadratic gravity, by a differential equation. Relations governing metrics with only constant-curvature $m$ dimensional subspaces are purely algebraic. We compare the two considered theories and study relations between their solution sets. We further examine conformal relations, generalized Petrov types, and compatibility with electromagnetic sources. Four- and six-dimensional cases are analyzed in detail, and so is the Weyl squared action (that reduces to Weyl conformal gravity in $n=4$), as a particular example of quadratic gravity couplings. Explicit analytic solutions illustrating the resulting structure are presented whenever possible.

papers.title: Challenging the hoop conjecture with spinning pancakes and baguettes
papers.authors: Robin Croft, Gerardo Garc\'ia-Moreno, Paolo Pani
papers.abstract: Understanding when gravitational collapse produces a black hole remains a central challenge in general relativity. Black-hole uniqueness results characterize the stationary endpoint under suitable assumptions, while singularity theorems establish geodesic incompleteness in the presence of trapped surfaces and appropriate energy and global conditions. Neither, however, provides a general criterion for horizon formation. The hoop conjecture offers such a criterion by relating the enclosed mass to the compactness of a matter distribution in every direction. We construct axisymmetric families of initial data describing rotating dust and test a formulation of the conjecture adapted to this setting. We explore highly prolate and oblate configurations with both constant and differential rescaled angular-velocity profiles, including configurations near the threshold for apparent-horizon formation. We find that the conjecture holds for rotating configurations, with a coefficient within 14% of unity as in the nonrotating case, provided the quasilocal mass includes the rotational energy. If the irreducible mass of the apparent horizon is used instead, the deviations grow with spin, as they do for Kerr black holes. For horizonless configurations, the conjecture likewise holds when the mass is restricted to the energy enclosed by the matter surface, whereas using the ADM mass, which also includes rotational field energy outside the matter, leads to apparent violations of up to $\approx$25%. We also discuss the possible evolution of compact configurations without apparent horizons, their relation to weak cosmic censorship, and their implications for horizonless compact objects.

papers.title: Sample complexity of learning fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states with single-copy and entangled measurements
papers.abstract: With single-copy measurements, every mixed fermionic Gaussian state on $m$ modes, pure modes included, is learned to trace distance $\epsilon$ from $\Theta(m^3/\epsilon^2)$ copies, with no logarithmic factor, against the known $\Theta(m^2/\epsilon^2)$ for collective measurements. We prove the upper bound, resolving Conjecture 10.1 of arXiv:2609.23189 (lower bound for $\epsilon\le1/3600$), and fill most open entries of the sample-complexity table of fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states, for single-copy, $k$-copy and collective measurements. With blocks of $k$ copies, the covariant highest-weight measurement of arXiv:2611.07271, read out through the Weyl-shift estimator, is exactly unbiased for every state; it gives $\Theta(\max\{m^3/k,m^2\}/\epsilon^2)$ in Frobenius norm on all states and in trace distance on every class at a fixed distance from the pure boundary. The gain $1/k$ ($k\le m$) away from the pure boundary, against $1/\sqrt k$ on cold number-conserving states, is therefore attained. Learning a quadratic fermionic Hamiltonian in Frobenius norm from its Gibbs state at bounded $\beta\|h\|$ has the same rate. For bosonic Gaussian states with bounded covariance, any displacement and squeezing, and occupations $n_1\le\dots\le n_m$, $O((m^2+r^3+\sum_{i,j>r}1/(n_i+n_j))/\epsilon^2)$ single-copy measurements suffice, $r$ the largest index with $r\,n_r\le2$; this is the minimax rate on dyadic-interval classes, with no spectral gap or cold-mode count assumed, and holds with no covariance bound for displaced passive states. With no bound on energy or squeezing, non-Gaussian measurements learn centred one-mode states, mixed included, from $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ and centred pure $m$-mode states from $O(m^2/\epsilon^2)$ single copies, free of the $\log\log E$ term of Gaussian measurements, and $m$-mode states from $O(m^3/\epsilon^2)$ copies, entangled only in a first round on blocks of $4m+6$.

papers.title: Maximal Violation of Mermin Inequality for Commuting von Neumann Algebras and Multipartite Vacuum Entanglement in QFT
papers.authors: Kan He, Jinchuan Hou, Shuyuan Yang, Bingke Zheng
papers.abstract: Summers and Werner proved that Bell inequalities are violated maximally and generically in the vacuum of a relativistic quantum field theory in [S. J. Summers and R. Werner, Commun. Math. Phys. 110 (1987), 247-259]. Their criterion concerns two-party case, that is, there are two algebras of quantum observables: one algebra and its commutant. In this case, the maximal CHSH value is converged to in every normal state exactly when the algebra is strongly stable. In the paper, we study the corresponding question for three and more mutually commuting von Neumann algebras. We focus on the multipartite Mermin inequalities instead of CHSH ones. For the tripartite Mermin functional we show that maximal violation in every normal state is equivalent to the existence of a common sequence of asymptotic GHZ stabilizers. Strong stability of each local factor is an necessary condition for maximal violation, and a joint embedding of an infinite GHZ tensor product is sufficient. Counterexamples show that strong stability and type III_1 of the individual algebras, even together with tripartite duality, do not suffice to arrive at the maximal violation. The results are also extended to n>=3 parties.

papers.title: A Neural Physics Solver for Richards Equation
papers.authors: Katherine MacKenzie, James Rand, Ben Ashby, Tristan Pryer, Claire E. Heaney, Christopher C. Pain, Thomas Rodding Kjeldsen
papers.abstract: A new approach to discretise and solve Richards equation based on the finite element method (FEM) is presented. The novelty of the approach, called the Neural Physics method, is that it expresses the discretisation as a convolution neural network (CNN) whose weights are predetermined by the integrals of the basis functions in the FEM. The Neural Physics method is physically consistent as it represents a discretisation of the governing equation and can run on CPUs, GPUs and the latest AI accelerators, resulting in an increase in computational speed. The Neural Physics method is demonstrated for two different discretisations of Richards equation, including a multigrid method that is realised through a U-Net architecture. The accuracy and speed of these methods is tested on a problem with a known analytical solution and compared to a standard FEM, and shows that the Neural Physics method is almost an order of magnitude faster than a comparable FEM. Finally, the Neural Physics method is applied to a real-world test case with integrated experimental data and simulates the infiltration of water through a rain garden. This new approach therefore provides a route to efficiently and accurately solve Richards equation for a wide array of hydrological applications.

papers.title: The multiplicative complexity of the three-bit low-half multiplier
papers.abstract: We prove that the multiplicative complexity of the three-bit low-half multiplier is six, giving a structural, enumeration-free lower-bound proof valid against unrestricted nonlinear reuse in Boolean XOR-AND circuits. The value was first established by SAT searches of the first author and independently confirmed by the second author. An explicit six-AND circuit supplies the upper bound. The lower bound combines derivatives, quadratic products, complementary minors, and extraction modulo a Boolean ideal. Independent finite checks accompany the arguments. $\mathrm{MC}(M_3)=6$ is fully formalized in Lean 4, using only Lean's three standard axioms (propositional extensionality, choice and quotient soundness).

papers.title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
papers.abstract: Symmetry is a foundational principle of physics: the behavior of a PDE-governed system does not depend on the coordinate frame, unit system, or mesh used to write it down, and neither should a surrogate model. Yet today's leading neural surrogates lack these invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem: for models trained on PDEs of cars in one pose (i.e., translation and rotation), rotating the full PDE raises the surface-pressure error from 4% to more than 100%, and re-sampling its boundary raises it to about 30%. We introduce ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a slice-attention transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs. Because the boundary determines the interior solution, ISLA encodes the posed boundary once into learned slices and evaluates arbitrary interior points independently through a tree-accelerated learned boundary kernel. Inputs are nondimensionalized in scales computed from the boundary, sums over boundary cells are area-weighted quadratures that converge under mesh refinement, and geometry enters only as distances and relative angles to equivariant slice anchors, making the model equivariant to rigid motions and reflections up to optional token subsampling and tree clustering. On AeroZoo, 2,816 3D flows spanning diverse geometries, poses, physical scales, and boundary conditions, ISLA's mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 1.9 and 2.2 times lower than any baseline's. On full AirfRANS, ISLA is second only to an explicit boundary-integral network (GLOBE), with errors at least 1.6 times lower than Transolver's and GeoTransolver's in every field.

papers.title: Fast mixing and thermal phases from strong decay of correlations
papers.abstract: We show that a strong form of correlation decay in quantum Gibbs states has far-reaching dynamical consequences. For a smooth path of geometrically local commuting Hamiltonians whose Gibbs states satisfy strong decay of correlations, we construct $\mathrm{O}(1)$-time quasi-local Lindbladian evolutions exactly connecting these states in both directions, together with $\mathrm{O}(1)$-time quasi-local Hamiltonian evolutions exactly connecting their canonical purifications. These quasi-local connections strengthen previously known quantum-channel circuit constructions based on the decay of connected correlation functions [R. Ma, V. Khemani, and S. Sang, PRX Quantum 7, 033052 (2026)], which approximately connect states within the same phase but have depths that grow logarithmically with system size. Furthermore, if the Gibbs-state path contains a product state, we prove that the single-site Glauber dynamics has a $\Omega(1)$ spectral gap independent of the system size throughout the path. This establishes Glauber-dynamics fast mixing for models that may violate the strong spatial mixing condition used in prior proofs, including (1) the $q$-state Potts model throughout the high-temperature phase for any $q$ and any finite dimension; (2) the Ising model with a longitudinal field at low temperature, with frustrating perturbations that destroy monotonicity of the dynamics; and (3) the three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory at low temperatures comparing to a field perturbation, even though the model supports classical memories at intermediate temperatures. Intriguingly, we establish fast mixing of these classical Markov chains using tools from quantum physics like Lieb-Robinson bounds.
